blocks.text: **The problem.** Build a stack on top of a plain array. Support `push(x)`, `pop()` (return the removed value, or **-1** if the stack is empty), `top()` (return the top value, or **-1** if empty), `isEmpty()` and `size()`.

blocks.alt: An array of capacity 6 holding 5, 8 and 3 in slots 0 to 2. A variable n equals 3: it counts the items and is also the index of the next free slot. The top of the stack is data[n - 1], which is 3.

blocks.code:
push(10)   push(20)   top()  -> 20
pop()      -> 20       pop()  -> 10
pop()      -> -1  (empty)       isEmpty() -> true

blocks.text: The whole question is **which end of the array is the top**. Pick the wrong end and every operation moves every element.
1. Brute force: the top at index 0

A natural first try: keep the top at the **front** of the array, like the top of a pile. But then pushing means making room at index 0 — shifting every item one place right — and popping shifts them all back.

blocks.alt: Pushing 7 when the top is at index 0: the items 3, 8 and 5 must each shift one slot right to make room, then 7 is written at index 0.

blocks.text: **push and pop are O(n).** Python's `insert(0, …)` and C++'s `insert(begin(), …)` hide the loop, but the shifting still happens. A stack whose push is O(n) has missed the point.
2. Optimal: the top at the end, with a fixed capacity

Flip it: keep the top at the **end**. Track `n`, the number of items. The top is `data[n - 1]`, push writes at `data[n]`, and pop just moves `n` back. Nothing ever shifts. This is the textbook stack — with one catch: the array has a **fixed capacity**, so a push into a full array is a **stack overflow**.
**Every operation is O(1)**, and space is O(capacity) whether you use it or not. Notice that pop doesn't erase anything — it just decrements `n`, and the next push overwrites the old value.

Keep the top at the end, but when the array is full, **grow** it: allocate an array **twice as big**, copy the items over, and carry on. That copy costs O(n) — but it happens so rarely that, averaged over all pushes, push is still **O(1)**. This is exactly how JavaScript arrays, Python lists, Java's `ArrayList` and C++'s `vector` grow.

blocks.alt: Doubling the capacity. A full array of 2 holding 10 and 20 is copied into a new array of 4; then 30 is pushed into slot 2. When that array of 4 fills up it is copied into an array of 8.

elements.text: copies so far: 2 + 4 + 8 + ... < 2n  ->  under 2 copies per push

blocks.caption: Push past the capacity and watch the array double. Popped values stay greyed out until they're overwritten.

blocks.text: **push is O(1) amortized, everything else O(1), space O(n).** Why amortized O(1)? To reach n items the array copied 2 + 4 + 8 + … + n items in total, which is less than 2n. Spread over n pushes, that's fewer than **2 copies per push**. (Doubling matters: growing by a fixed +10 each time would make the copies add up to O(n²).)

rows.approach: Brute force: the top at index 0
rows.timeWhy: Every push and pop **shifts all the items** by one.

rows.approach: Optimal: the top at the end, with a fixed capacity
rows.timeWhy: Push and pop just **move the top index**.
A rare **doubling** copies 2 + 4 + … + n < **2n** items in total: O(1) per push on average.
rows.spaceWhy: The array is never more than **twice** the items.

items: **pop and top on an empty stack** — return -1, don't crash.
**Push exactly up to the capacity, then one more** — the growth must copy every item, in order.
**Pop, then push** — the new value overwrites the stale slot.
**Interleaved pushes and pops** — `size()` must always equal pushes minus successful pops.

blocks.text: **Follow-up:** some implementations also **shrink** the array (halve it when it's only a quarter full) so memory follows the stack back down. Shrinking at **half** full instead would cause thrashing — alternating push/pop at the boundary would copy every time.
